summary: Defines a SIP media feature tag that lets a user agent say which MIME application subtypes it can handle. Callers can then use caller preferences to reach a device that supports the kind of application they want to use in a session. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: Before sending a package, you might want to know whether the other side has the right tool to open it. This tag lets a phone announce which kinds of application data it can handle.

questions: sip media feature tag for mime application subtypes
how does sip indicate supported application types
what is a sip media feature tag
how does sip route calls by capability
subtitle: A SIP media feature tag that lets a device say which application streaming formats it can handle.

tldr.problem: SIP already lets a device advertise that it supports the application media type, but that is too coarse, since applications such as games and whiteboards are wildly different.
tldr.mechanism: The new sip.app-subtype media feature tag lists the MIME application subtypes a user agent can stream, so registrations and caller preferences can match on them.
tldr.outcome: A caller can be routed to a device that supports the specific application stream wanted, instead of any device with some application support.

today: RFC 5688 is a Proposed Standard, published in January 2010, and the metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It extends the media feature tags of RFC 3840.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
SIP caller preferences (RFC 3841) let a caller state what kind of device it wants to reach. A user agent records its own capabilities when it registers (RFC 3840), and a proxy compares the caller's preferences against the stored registrations to choose targets. RFC 3840 expresses capabilities as media feature tags, each with a name and a type.

RFC 3840 defines one tag per top-level media type, such as sip.audio and sip.video. The motivating example is a videophone call: it should ring the user's videophone first and only fall back to an audio-only mobile if the user is not on the videophone.
sections.eli5: When you call someone with two devices, the call should go to the one that can do what you want, like a video call to the one with a screen.

sections.title: Why the Application Tag Is Too Coarse
sections.content:
The application media type covers an extremely broad range of subtypes, such as multiplayer games, shared whiteboards and application sharing. With audio and video, agents often share a common codec, so routing to any device that supports audio is likely to work.

Application streams are different. Routing a request to an agent that supports some application stream is not useful, because application streams for different applications are wildly different. The specific subtype has to be indicated as well, and this RFC defines a new tag for that purpose.
sections.eli5: Knowing a device can play some game is useless if it cannot play the game you picked. You need the game's name.

sections.title: The sip.app-subtype Tag
sections.content:
The sip.app-subtype tag has type token with a case-insensitive equality relationship. Its value can be any registered or private MIME application subtype that fits the subtype-name grammar of RFC 4288.

In the Contact header field of a REGISTER request, an agent SHOULD list all application subtypes it can support as streaming formats. A subtype counts as supported if the agent could process an SDP offer containing that subtype as a format in the m-line. In Accept-Contact or Reject-Contact, the tag says the caller wants to reach, or avoid, an agent that can stream using that subtype.

The tag only describes streaming media. It says nothing about what the agent does itself, or about the MIME types it can send or receive in SIP messages or emails. For a body of type application/example in a SIP request, the agent would use the type tag from RFC 3840 instead. New streaming formats SHOULD be defined using the SDP application stream and a MIME application subtype.
sections.eli5: The tag is a list of the exact games a phone can stream. It is not a promise about anything else the phone can do.

sections.title: Registration and Matching Example
sections.content:
The RFC's example shows a REGISTER whose Contact header carries +sip.app-subtype="example" beside tags such as audio, schemes and class. This means the agent can take part in application sessions that exchange application/example objects.

An INVITE whose SDP has an audio line and the line m=application 8493 udp example would be accepted by that agent. The SDP describes an audio session plus an application session running over UDP.
sections.eli5: The phone signs in saying it can play a game called example. When someone invites it to play that game, it says yes.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
In a REGISTER, the tag reveals which application media streams the device supports. That may be sensitive, because it gives insight into the capabilities of a product. The concerns already discussed in RFC 3840 apply here as well.

Applications using the tag SHOULD provide a means of ensuring its integrity. It should be trusted only when it comes from the user or user agent it describes, so mechanisms for conveying it SHOULD guarantee authenticity.
sections.eli5: A list of what your phone can do tells strangers about it, and it should only be believed if it really came from your phone.

sections.title: IANA Registration
sections.content:
The RFC adds sip.app-subtype to the SIP Media Feature Tag Registration Tree defined in RFC 3840, with ASN.1 identifier 1.3.6.1.8.4.24. The value type is token with an equality relationship.

The registration says the tag is most useful in communications applications for describing the capabilities of a device such as a phone or PDA. Its example of typical use is routing a call to a phone that can support a multiplayer game.
sections.eli5: The tag's name was written in the official list so nobody else uses it for something different.
